terms.d: Stack, queue, linked lists — order and access rules matter.
Asymptotics, recurrence, Master theorem — how cost grows with n.
Compare algorithms by time, space, and stability.

concepts: Module 1 flow: structures → analysis → divide-and-conquer → sorts.
Exam style: define + complexity + one contrast (e.g. stack vs queue).
notes: LMR first: Stack, postfix, Tower of Hanoi.
Never give only a name — always add LIFO/FIFO or Big-O when asked.

terms.d: Hierarchical linked structures; BST/AVL/B-tree variants balance search cost.
Vertices + edges; DFS/BFS and shortest paths are core traversals.

concepts: Trees first, then graph traversals and path algorithms.
Prim vs Kruskal both build MSTs — different selection rules.
notes: LMR: binary tree / BST basics before AVL/B-tree detail.

terms.d: Optimal substructure + overlapping subproblems; store results.
Locally optimal choice hoping for global optimum — not always correct.
Knapsack variants, activity selection, Huffman, TSP.

concepts: 0/1 knapsack → DP; fractional knapsack → greedy — classic exam trap.
TSP is typically hard; don’t treat it as a simple greedy always.
notes: LMR: DP approach, optimality principle, Strassen.

terms.d: Find pattern P in text T — naïve vs Rabin–Karp hashing.
Vertex cover, set cover, subset-sum — often near-optimal algorithms.

concepts: Rabin–Karp uses rolling hash; naïve compares character by character.
Vertex cover / set cover are classic approximation settings.
notes: LMR: naïve matching, Rabin–Karp, vertex cover.

terms.d: Hard decision problems; reductions show hardness.
Visit each vertex once and return — classic NP-complete flavour.
Efficiency/resource angle linked in this module’s framing.

concepts: NP-complete vs NP-hard: completeness is in NP + hard for NP.
Reducibility is the proof tool — map known hard problem to yours.
notes: LMR: NP proofs / reducibility vocabulary.

terms.d: LIFO structure: push/pop at the same end (the top).
Insert an element on top.
Remove the top element.
Read the top without removing it.
Pop on empty / push on full (array stack).

concepts: Stack ≠ queue: LIFO vs FIFO.
Call stack / undo / postfix evaluation are classic uses.
Array stack needs capacity; linked stack grows with nodes.
notes: Trap: do not say FIFO for stack.
Stem “last in first out / top only” → stack.
LMR: define + one use + contrast with queue.

terms.d: Operators follow their operands (e.g. 3 4 +).
Scan left→right: push operands; on operator, pop args, push result.
Defers operators until operands are known — natural LIFO.

concepts: Infix needs precedence/parentheses; postfix does not.
Each operator pops the right number of operands (usually 2 for binary).
notes: Trap: processing order is left to right, not ‘operator first’.
If expression is infix, convert first — don’t evaluate infix with raw postfix rules.
LMR: walk one tiny example on paper.

terms.d: Move n disks from source to target using auxiliary peg.
Only one disk at a time; never place larger on smaller.

concepts: Recursive idea: move n−1 aside, move largest, move n−1 on top.
Shows divide-and-conquer / recursion cost explosion.
notes: Trap: minimum moves are 2^n−1, not n^2.
LMR: state recurrence + closed form.

terms.d: FIFO: enqueue at rear, dequeue at front.
Insert rear / remove front.
Wrap indices to reuse array space.

concepts: Queue ≠ stack (FIFO vs LIFO).
BFS uses a queue; DFS uses a stack/recursion.
notes: Trap: don’t pop from rear for a normal queue.
Stem “first come first served” → queue.

terms.d: Nodes with data + pointer(s); dynamic size.
Each node points to next only.
Entry pointer to the first node.

concepts: Insert/delete can be O(1) given a node reference; search is O(n).
Vs array: no random access O(1), but flexible growth.
notes: Trap: linked list ≠ array contiguous memory.
Always track head (and sometimes tail) carefully.

terms.d: Each node has next and prev pointers.
Walk forward or backward.
Easier deletion when you have the node (prev is known).

concepts: Extra pointer cost vs singly linked.
Still no O(1) index access like arrays.
notes: Trap: update both next and prev on insert/delete — half-updates break the list.

terms.d: Finite, unambiguous sequence of steps producing output from input.
Input, output, finiteness, definiteness, effectiveness (and often generality).

concepts: Program implements an algorithm in a language.
Finiteness: must terminate; definiteness: each step clear.
notes: Trap: infinite loop is not a valid algorithm characteristic.

terms.d: Upper bound on growth rate (worst-case flavour in teaching).
Lower bound on growth.
Tight bound — both O and Ω.
Stricter / asymptotic equivalence ideas (if taught).

concepts: Asymptotics ignore constants and lower-order terms.
O(n^2) does not mean ‘exactly n^2 steps’.
notes: Trap: O is not the same as Θ unless also Ω.
Spelling in syllabus: ‘Asymtotic’ = asymptotic notations.

terms.d: How running time grows with input size n.
Different cases; exams often want worst-case Big-O.
Extra memory growth with n.

concepts: Count dominant operations, not wall-clock alone.
Nested loops often multiply costs.
notes: Trap: ‘faster machine’ does not change asymptotic class.

terms.d: T(n) defined in terms of T(smaller).
Strategies to solve recurrences.
Stops recursion; needed for well-founded analysis.

concepts: Wrong base case ⇒ wrong closed form.
Unfold a few levels before guessing the pattern.
notes: Trap: forgetting the +f(n) combine cost in divide-and-conquer.

terms.d: Solves T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n) for many standard f.
Compare f(n) with n^{log_b a} (three main cases).
Not all recurrences fit; need regularity conditions.

concepts: Identify a, b, f(n) first — then case.
Merge sort: a=2,b=2,f=Θ(n) → Θ(n log n).
notes: Trap: applying Master when split is uneven or f doesn’t fit cases.

terms.d: Divide → conquer recursively → combine.
Often T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n).
Merge sort, binary search, some matrix methods.

concepts: Combine cost f(n) matters as much as subproblem count.
Not every recursive algorithm is efficient D&C.
notes: Trap: confusing D&C with DP (DP stores overlapping results).

terms.d: Repeatedly swap adjacent out-of-order pairs.
O(n^2) typical/worst; can be O(n) if already sorted with early exit.
Can be implemented stable.

concepts: Simple but slow for large n.
After pass i, largest elements ‘bubble’ to the end.
notes: Trap: don’t claim O(n log n) for bubble sort.

terms.d: Build sorted prefix; insert next element into place.
O(n^2) worst; O(n) best on nearly sorted data.
Yes (typical implementation).

concepts: Good for small or nearly sorted arrays.
Online: can sort as data arrives.
notes: Trap: best-case O(n) ≠ average O(n).

terms.d: Repeatedly select min (or max) from unsorted part and swap into place.
Θ(n^2) comparisons roughly always.
Typical swap-based version is unstable.

concepts: Fewer writes than some sorts, but still quadratic comparisons.
Unlike insertion, does not benefit much from nearly sorted input.
notes: Trap: selection ≠ insertion — selection always scans remaining min.

terms.d: Divide array, sort halves, merge sorted runs.
Θ(n log n) guaranteed.
Needs Θ(n) auxiliary for classic merge.
Yes.

concepts: Predictable performance — good exam ‘guaranteed n log n’ answer.
Merge is the combine step.
notes: Trap: merge sort is not in-place in the standard form.

terms.d: Build heap, repeatedly extract max/min.
O(n log n).
Yes (array heap); not typically stable.

concepts: Uses heap property: parent ordered vs children.
Build-heap is O(n); extracts cost O(n log n).
notes: Trap: heap sort ≠ priority-queue ADT lecture alone — it’s a sorting algorithm.

terms.d: Partition around pivot; recurse on parts.
O(n log n); worst O(n^2) on bad pivots.
Mostly yes (small stack); not stable typically.

concepts: Pivot choice affects balance.
Often fastest in practice despite worst case.
notes: Trap: worst case is quadratic — mention randomised/median-of-three if asked.

terms.d: Connected acyclic graph; hierarchical parent–child.
Top node / no children / has children.
File systems, expression trees, search structures, heaps.

concepts: Tree ≠ general graph with cycles.
Height/depth definitions vary slightly — use syllabus convention.
notes: LMR: terminology first before BST/AVL detail.
Trap: ‘tree’ in CS usually means rooted tree in DSA units.

terms.d: Each node has at most two children (left/right).
Variants about occupancy of levels (syllabus defs).
Inorder, preorder, postorder, level-order.

concepts: Binary tree ≠ BST (BST adds ordering invariant).
Array representation possible for complete trees (heaps).
notes: LMR: define binary tree + name three DFS-style traversals.
Trap: don’t assume sorted order without BST property.

terms.d: Left keys < node < right keys (standard ordering).
Follow comparisons down a path.
Yields keys in sorted order.

concepts: Balanced BST ⇒ O(log n); skewed ⇒ O(n).
Deletion has cases: leaf / one child / two children (successor/predecessor).
notes: LMR: state ordering invariant clearly.
Trap: binary tree without order is not a BST.

terms.d: BST arranged to minimise expected search cost given key probabilities.
Classic dynamic-programming optimisation on key ranges.

concepts: Not the same as ‘any balanced BST’ — optimality uses frequencies.
Related to matrix-chain style interval DP.
notes: Trap: AVL/Red-Black balance ≠ probability-optimal BST.

terms.d: Self-balancing BST with coloured nodes and rotation/recolour rules.
Height O(log n); operations O(log n).

concepts: Alternative to AVL with slightly different balance strictness.
Used widely in libraries (e.g. some map implementations).
notes: Trap: colour rules are invariants — don’t invent ‘just paint randomly’.

terms.d: BST where |height(left)−height(right)| ≤ 1 at every node.
LL, RR, LR, RL fix imbalance after insert/delete.
Search/insert/delete O(log n).

concepts: Stricter balance than Red-Black often ⇒ more rotations.
Balance factor is the height difference.
notes: Trap: AVL is a BST plus height invariant — not a heap.

terms.d: Multiway balanced search tree for disk/block storage.
Many keys per node ⇒ shallow tree ⇒ fewer disk reads.
All leaves at same level; node occupancy bounds (order).

concepts: Designed for secondary storage, not only RAM.
B+ trees (if taught) keep data in leaves — don’t conflate blindly.
notes: Trap: B-tree ≠ binary tree; ‘B’ is not ‘binary’.

terms.d: Subgraph that is a tree connecting all vertices.
Spanning tree of minimum total edge weight.

concepts: Exists for connected undirected graphs.
Prim/Kruskal compute MSTs.
notes: Trap: spanning tree has V−1 edges — no cycles.

terms.d: Grow MST from a start vertex by always adding lightest safe edge out.
Often priority queue for cut edges.

concepts: Cut property: lightest edge crossing the cut is safe for MST.
Prim is vertex-centric growth.
notes: Trap: Prim ≠ Kruskal (Kruskal sorts edges globally).

terms.d: Sort edges by weight; add if it doesn’t form a cycle (Union–Find).
Tracks components to detect cycles efficiently.

concepts: Edge-centric; works well on sparse graphs.
Same MST cut/cycle properties as Prim’s goal.
notes: Trap: adding lightest edge blindly without cycle check is wrong.

terms.d: G=(V,E); directed/undirected; weighted/unweighted.
Adjacency matrix vs adjacency list.
Systematic visit: DFS/BFS.

concepts: Matrix: O(1) edge query, O(V^2) space; list: better for sparse.
Degree, path, cycle are core terms.
notes: Trap: pick representation based on density — not always matrix.

terms.d: Explore deep along a path; backtrack; stack/recursion.
Cycle detect, topological sort, components, path finding.

concepts: DFS forest / timestamps appear in CLRS-style analysis.
Not optimal shortest path in weighted graphs by itself.
notes: Trap: DFS ≠ BFS order; DFS not for unweighted shortest path.

terms.d: Explore level by level using a queue.
BFS layers give fewest edges from source.

concepts: Queue is essential; mark visited to avoid reprocessing.
Contrast with Dijkstra for weighted graphs.
notes: Trap: BFS on weighted edges with different weights ≠ Dijkstra.

terms.d: Shortest paths from one source to all vertices.
Non-negative weights; greedy with priority queue.
Handles negative edges; detects negative cycles.

concepts: Dijkstra fails with negative edges.
Relaxation is the common primitive.
notes: Trap: using Dijkstra with negatives — wrong.

terms.d: Shortest paths between every pair.
DP over intermediate vertices; O(V^3).
Reweighting + Dijkstra from each source.

concepts: Floyd works with negatives but not negative cycles.
Matrix DP update: d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][k]+d[k][j]).
notes: Trap: Floyd ≠ single BFS from each node on weighted graphs.

terms.d: Solve overlapping subproblems once; store answers.
Top-down cache vs bottom-up table.
Optimal substructure + overlapping subproblems.

concepts: DP ≠ divide-and-conquer alone (D&C may not overlap).
DP ≠ greedy (greedy never revisits choices systematically).
notes: LMR: say both conditions for DP.
Trap: calling every recursion ‘DP’ without storage of overlaps.

terms.d: Optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems.
Justifies composing sub-results into global optimum.

concepts: If principle fails, DP formulation is invalid.
Check on a small example before coding a table.
notes: LMR: one-line definition of optimality principle.
Trap: optimality principle ≠ ‘greedy choice property’ (that’s greedy).

terms.d: Faster matrix multiply than naïve O(n^3) using 7 recursive multiplies.
Algebraic recombination reduces multiplications; adds more additions.

concepts: Asymptotically better; constants/practicality may vary.
Still divide-and-conquer on quadrants.
notes: LMR: ‘7 products instead of 8’ is the memorable fact.
Trap: Strassen is not related to shortest paths.

terms.d: Parenthesise matrix product to minimise scalar multiplies.
Interval DP over chain length.

concepts: Order of multiplication changes cost, not the mathematical product.
Classic DP table m[i][j].
notes: Trap: this is about cost of parenthesisation — not Strassen’s algorithm itself.

terms.d: Longest common subsequence of two strings (not necessarily contiguous).
If chars equal, diagonal+1; else max of skip either.

concepts: Subsequence ≠ substring (substring is contiguous).
Used in diff tools / bioinformatics examples.
notes: Trap: LCS vs longest common substring — contiguousness.

terms.d: Each item take or not; maximise value under weight limit.
dp[i][w] style; pseudo-polynomial in capacity.
Cannot break items.

concepts: Contrast fractional knapsack (greedy by value/weight).
NP-hard as optimisation in general; DP works for integer capacity.
notes: Trap: using greedy value/weight for 0/1 — incorrect in general.

terms.d: Build solution by locally best choice at each step.
Local optimum can lead to global (when algorithm is correct).
Proof style that swaps to show optimality.

concepts: Greedy is fast but not always optimal — need a proof or known pattern.
Examples: activity selection, Huffman, fractional knapsack.
notes: Trap: ‘greedy always works’ — false.

terms.d: Select max non-overlapping activities.
Usually earliest finishing time first.

concepts: Sort by finish time, then pick compatible next.
Classic proof via greedy choice + optimal substructure.
notes: Trap: sorting by start time alone is not the standard optimal greedy.

terms.d: Optimal prefix codes using frequency-greedy tree.
No codeword is prefix of another — unique decode.
Repeatedly merge two least frequent nodes.

concepts: More frequent symbols → shorter codes.
Related to binary trees and priority queues.
notes: Trap: Huffman is for encoding efficiency — not encryption security.

terms.d: May take fraction of an item.
Sort by value/weight ratio; take until capacity fills.

concepts: Optimal for fractional case; not for 0/1.
Last item may be taken partially.
notes: Trap: applying fractional greedy to 0/1 knapsack.

terms.d: Visit each city once and return; minimise tour length.
Classic NP-hard optimisation problem.
Brute force, DP (Held–Karp), heuristics/approx.

concepts: Brute force is factorial — not scalable.
Don’t claim a simple greedy always optimal for general TSP.
notes: Trap: confusing TSP with MST (MST is not a tour).

terms.d: Select items under capacity to maximise value.
0/1, fractional, unbounded — different algorithms.

concepts: Name the variant before choosing DP vs greedy.
Syllabus may revisit knapsack under ‘problems’ cluster.
notes: Trap: one word ‘knapsack’ — always specify 0/1 vs fractional.

terms.d: Schedule jobs to maximise profit under constraints (often deadlines/slots).
Often sort by profit; place in latest free slot before deadline.

concepts: Related to deadline scheduling themes.
Check whether multiple slots / unit time jobs assumed.
notes: Trap: sequencing ≠ OS process scheduling vocabulary unless syllabus links them.

terms.d: Unit-time jobs with deadlines and profits; maximise profit.
Sort profits descending; assign to feasible time slot.

concepts: Feasibility: finish by deadline.
Greedy placement into latest possible slot is common.
notes: Trap: ignoring deadline when taking highest profit first blindly.

terms.d: Try P at every shift of T; compare chars.
O((n−m+1)m) worst case.

concepts: Simple baseline for Rabin–Karp / KMP comparisons.
Many mismatches still cost comparisons.
notes: LMR: state complexity clearly.
Trap: naïve is not hashing-based.

terms.d: Rolling hash of windows; verify on hash hit.
Hash match but strings differ — must verify.
Good with strong hash; worst can degrade.

concepts: Rolling hash updates in O(1) per shift.
Multiple patterns can share hashing ideas.
notes: LMR: hash then verify — never skip verify.
Trap: hash equality ≠ string equality.

terms.d: Set of vertices incident to every edge.
Classic 2-approx: pick both ends of an uncovered edge, repeat.

concepts: Decision version is NP-complete; approx is taught for algorithms design.
Minimal vs minimum — wording matters.
notes: LMR: definition + idea of 2-approximation.
Trap: vertex cover ≠ vertex colouring.

terms.d: Cover universe with minimum number of subsets.
Repeatedly pick set covering most remaining elements.

concepts: NP-hard; greedy gives logarithmic approximation classically.
Related to hitting-set formulations.
notes: Trap: set cover ≠ vertex cover (different universe structure).

terms.d: Algorithms that use randomness for speed/simplicity (expected performance).
Optimise linear objective under linear constraints — algorithmic tool.

concepts: Syllabus pairs ideas for advanced design techniques.
Randomised algorithms need expected/high-probability analysis.
notes: Trap: randomised ≠ incorrect; analyse failure probability.

terms.d: Is there a subset summing to target t?
NP-complete decision; pseudo-poly DP possible.

concepts: Related to knapsack decision version.
Meet-in-the-middle sometimes taught for moderate n.
notes: Trap: subset-sum ≠ always polynomial — depends on numeric magnitude.

terms.d: Efficiency/resource-conscious computing themes tied to algorithmic cost.
Fewer operations / less energy as a motivation for better algorithms.

concepts: Treat as syllabus framing unless SLM gives a narrower definition.
Connect to choosing efficient algorithms over naïve ones.
notes: LMR: one line linking green goals to algorithmic efficiency.
Trap: don’t invent unrelated ecology essays — stay CS-framed.

terms.d: Cycle visiting each vertex exactly once and returning.
Deciding existence is NP-complete (classic).

concepts: Vs Euler tour: Euler uses every edge; Hamiltonian every vertex.
TSP optimisation builds on Hamiltonian ideas.
notes: LMR: vertex-once cycle definition + NP-complete mention.
Trap: Hamiltonian ≠ Eulerian.

terms.d: Show problem in NP + polynomial reduction from known NP-complete problem.
Short verifiable witness for yes instances (for NP).

concepts: Reduction direction: known hard ≤p your problem.
Polynomial-time verification ≠ polynomial-time solving.
notes: LMR: two parts of a completeness proof.
Trap: reducing your problem to SAT shows yours is ‘no harder’ — wrong direction for hardness.

terms.d: Hardest problems in NP (under poly reductions).
SAT, vertex cover decision, Hamiltonian cycle, subset-sum, …

concepts: If any NP-complete problem has poly algorithm, P=NP.
Practice recognising ‘decision version’ wording.
notes: Trap: optimisation TSP vs decision Hamiltonian — related but not identical statements.

terms.d: At least as hard as NP-complete; may not be in NP.
Satisfiability of Boolean formulas — central NP-complete problem.

concepts: NP-hard includes problems outside NP (e.g. some optimisation/undecidable-adjacent teaching examples).
SAT is the usual reduction source.
notes: Trap: NP-hard ≠ NP-complete unless also in NP.

terms.d: Problem A ≤p B if A transforms to B in poly time.
B is at least as hard as A (for hardness proofs).

concepts: Cook–Levin historically links SAT to NP-completeness theory.
Always state what reduces to what.
notes: Trap: arrow direction mistakes fail proofs.
